category_title: Artistically-inclined students who adapt storytelling skills to technical 3D modeling
minimal_context: The student is working on adding interactive game assets and obstacles to their 'Wheels on Fire' game level in the 3D Animation and Gaming track.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's review your 'Wheels on Fire' game level. Your classmates mentioned there isn't much for players to do yet, so please start adding interactive game assets and obstacles.

STUDENT: I've been focusing on the environment. Since my school is by Fisherman's Wharf, I go there a lot and know how it should look. I just finished recreating the Golden Gate Bridge.

TUTOR: That looks fine, but what about the interactive parts of the game?

STUDENT: Well, someone observed that my early renderings were too flat, so I've been using the lighting tools to include shadows from the bridge and bike to create a better 3D effect.

TUTOR: You need to focus on the gameplay now. What obstacles are you going to add for the player?

STUDENT: I know peers said there isn't much for players to do, but I am most proud of the landmarks in my game right now. Honestly, I just wish I had time to add more scenery, like a silhouette of the San Francisco skyline, instead of figuring out how to add cars or pedestrians.

options.A: List goals for the sessions, such as being vocal, expressing ideas, speaking comfortably in front of a group, and accepting constructive criticism.
options.B: Implement relatively tight timelines for adding the interactive game assets and obstacles during the production phase of the game project.
options.C: Provide an anchored experience through a class visit to Fisherman's Wharf and take photos to use as visual prompts for the game level.
options.D: Frame students as 'developers helping game studios' and justify mundane tasks like placing obstacles by comparing them to professional gaming standards.
